children: "I think where we have started to really synthesize what's happening in the AI and the data center build out is, are we moving to a too-big-to-fail AI ecosystem?" said Jeffrey Schmid, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.
"I think that's where some of our data is trying to focus itself: Is there anything systemic? I mean, kind of back to the Silicon Valley experience," he noted.

"Trying to address these things is a little difficult for the Fed to do. It's much more of a fiscal action," Schmid said. "There's a lot of political debate going on right now about how do you manage this AI phenomenon going forward."
Schmid was speaking on "The Federal Reserve, Financial Innovation, and Economic Development" before the Civic Council of Greater Kansas City meeting.

On the blockchain technology, Schmid thinks the blockchain technology makes sense, especially in the banking business. "Is there a way to create a blockchain that can actually tokenize deposits and allow the transaction to go 24/7 or cross border with less friction."
On inflation, he said, "We still haven't fixed the inflation issue. We're still in the more than five years of inflation above target."
On disruption in payment technologies, Schmid said over the next few years, it will likely be in fees for payments, such as the fees that you pay to Visa
to process a transaction. "And, it's going to get to a point where everything is instantaneous because settlement will be down to really hyper sectors."

"That's going to change the nature of what happens. I mean, we're seeing actually companies start to go to things like day pay. You work a day, you get paid. And the more that is integrated in the system, the more you're going to see demands from the workforce to say, 'Why do I have to wait two weeks for me to get paid? I'd like to get paid every day'."

"As regulators, we are going to worry less about capital and more about liquidity because the nature and speed of payments are going to really put a different kind of lens on how you manage your balance," he noted.

"Instant payments will leap over all of the hybrid technology. It could take four or five more years to do that, but something could happen from a policy standpoint that accelerates that," he said during the Q&A.

title: Kansas City Fed's Schmid: Are we moving to a too-big-to-fail AI ecosystem?
